newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korean famine aid efforts gather pace.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean famine aid efforts gather pace.

text.p: International relief efforts for North Korea gathered pace on Tuesday as fears about its military intentions gave way to urgent action to avert the "hell" of a severe famine.

Underscoring the urgency, North Korea told aid agencies in Pyongyang that 134 children had died of malnutrition so far in the country's food crisis, the first figure it has given on deaths, according to Hans Olsen of the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF speaking in Geneva.

In response to the crisis, the first direct sale of American grain to the Stalinist nation since the 1950-53 Korean War was disclosed and in capitalist South Korea religious and civic groups announced plans to ship 110,000 tonnes of corn to their communist brethren.
A U.S. congressman just back from North Korea said in Tokyo on Tuesday he saw soldiers whose uniforms hung off their bodies, showing Pyongyang's elite military was suffering.
"North Korea is rapidly descending into a hell of severe famine," U.S. Congressman Tony Hall, a Democrat from Ohio, told reporters after returning from a four-day tour of North Korea.

Hall gave a bleak account of wide areas of northwestern North Korea where gaunt women and children scrounged for "anything that looked edible" in depleted soil in a landscape where every tree had been cut down for firewood.
"You look at the soldiers and their uniforms don't fit," he told reporters "Everyone is systematically starving together."

Many countries have been slow to respond to international appeals for food aid to North Korea out of fears that donations would be diverted to the 1.1 million-strong armed forces, who consume about a quarter of the impoverished state's budget.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, on a visit to Japan, voiced the fears when he told reporters the situation in North Korea was unstable and the United States was having a difficult time assessing the extent of hunger.
He denied the United States was using food as a weapon by its cautious response to reports of the famine.
"Our policy is not to either feed fat generals or to starve innocent people, but rather to be of help where humanitarian assistance can be helpful," Cohen said.

However, giant U.S. grain trader Cargill Inc.'s announcement that it had reached agreement with North Korea to supply wheat and growing relief efforts by South Korea, indicated that the tide was turning towards an all-out effort to help Pyongyang.
In Seoul, traders close to the Cargill deal said North Korea had agreed to barter about 4,000 tonnes of zinc for about 20,000 tonnes of wheat.
U.S. officials said it was the first direct sale of U.S. grown wheat to North Korea since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War, when Washington imposed a ban on trade with Pyongyang.
Apart from Tuesday's action by religious groups, the South Korean Red Cross last week sent more than $1 million worth of food and vegetable seed to North Korea.
Separately last week, the Seoul government lifted a ban on private organisations providing rice to Pyongyang and allowed local business groups to join food aid programmes.
Previously, only local religious and civic groups and individual South Koreans could ship non-rice food aid. Seoul had maintained rice could be diverted to the military.
The Seoul moves were an apparent bid to lure the North to peace talks among the two Koreas, China and the United States.
The talks are aimed at securing a peace treaty to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

U.S. officials say North Korea has told Washington it would soon decide whether to join the peace talks and believe Pyongyang had been positively influenced by the "cumulative affect" of recent food aid appeals.
The World Food Programme has said North Korea faces a grain shortage of 2.3 million tonnes this year.

The chairman of the U.S. military Joint Chiefs of Staff met his South Korean counterpart on Tuesday to discuss the threat from North Korea as it grapples with the food crisis, a Seoul military official said.
John Shalikashvili arrived in South Korea earlier on Tuesday for a two-day visit, which will overlap with a trip to Seoul by U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen.

Shalikashvili and Yoon Yong-nam discussed security on the Korean peninsula and steps to hone readiness against any attack from North Korea, said a spokesman for the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea to defend against the communist North.

Shalikashvili and Yoon "agreed North Korea was in a state of crisis due to a severe food shortage and pledged their two countries would cooperate to defend against any emergency situation on the peninsula", the spokesman said.
However, U.S. officials insist they have no evidence of unusual military movements in the North.
